source.title: What Does Alignment Cost? The Structural Brittleness of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
source.authors: Joanna Hao; Shanduojiao Jiang; Sailaja Nakka

record.tranche_reason: Tests self-repair using dual-direction resample ablation of dynamically discovered attention-head circuits, with a different setup from the original Hydra-effect work.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ablation results for discovered multi-head circuits, not individual-head or layer ablations. Circuit head counts used to define the intervention are not outcome rows. The paper also reports denoising sufficiency scores, but those measure recovery when a circuit is injected into a corrupted context, not compensation after ablation; they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study resample-noises multi-head circuits chosen by single-head patching and reports only the total drop in logit difference (2.92% Base, 6.79% Instruct on synthetic tasks). It reads the small drop, next to roughly 100% denoising sufficiency, as the Hydra effect. It never measures a direct effect, any downstream component's change, or later-layer compensation. The small total effect can't be told apart from plain redundancy, or from the 80% threshold leaving out heads that carry the computation in parallel. The backup-circuit account is asserted, not measured. This is a related construct (robustness of total effect, or necessity/sufficiency asymmetry), not a measured rate of self-repair, so it goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim, without measuring it, that later-layer 'backup circuits' recompute the corrupted logic, i.e. the Hydra effect. They frame instruction tuning as an 'Alignment Tax on Redundancy' that repurposes these backup heads.
record.recipe_differences: Uses dynamic single-head activation patching to select circuits, followed by dual-direction resample ablation of the selected multi-head circuits; evaluates naturally successful CoT traces and compares a base and instruction-tuned model.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured necessity drop varies by task and model: the Instruct model is more affected on the synthetic average, while the two models have similar drops on GSM8K Proxy. Circuit discovery is conditioned on the 8-shot prompt template.

fits_no_version.finding: Resample-noising a dynamically selected head circuit cuts the clean logit difference by only 0.4–8%, although denoising the same circuit restores about 99–100%. Instruct's synthetic average drop (6.79%) is larger than Base's (2.92%); on the GSM8K proxy the two are similar (5.10% vs 4.96%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Asymmetry between necessity and sufficiency of attention-head circuits (redundancy / total-effect robustness) and its change after instruction tuning.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 4th Workshop on Towards Knowledgeable Foundation Models (KnowFM 2026)
record.problems: Evidence is restricted to a within-family comparison at 1B parameters and uses procedurally generated tasks, including a GSM8K proxy. Results are conditioned on one 8-shot prompt template and on instances the models solved correctly before intervention. The paper does not report uncertainty estimates. It does not directly isolate backup heads or measure downstream compensation layer by layer.
record.rows_left_out: No more than 60 rows were reported. Denoising sufficiency percentages and circuit head counts were left out: the former measures recovery after injecting a circuit into corrupted contexts rather than compensation after ablation, and the latter is used to set intervention size.

untested.parts: No layer-level ablation and no measure of later attention layers restoring output.
No MLP interventions or measurements (stated out of scope).
No single-head ablation with direct versus total effect, and no general text. Only multi-head circuits in one 1B Llama family on synthetic and proxy tasks.
No compensation fraction, prompt-level variability or overcorrection measured.
Backup heads are invoked but never identified or ablated; no copy-suppression, LayerNorm or anti-erasure analysis.
Resample ablation is used, but self-repair isn't measured under any ablation, and there is no zero-ablation comparison.
No attribution scores are compared against a measure of what components actually do.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 and its supports labels rest on reading small total effects as compensation, which the design can't establish. Circuits are defined as heads covering 80% of single-head restorative impact, so the remaining heads may carry the computation in parallel. Circuit sizes differ between models (average 57 vs 95 heads on synthetic tasks), confounding the Base/Instruct comparison. The reported averages don't match the per-task means. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No layer-level ablation or measurement of later attention layers restoring the output.
No late-MLP measurements, maximum-likelihood-token downregulation, or earlier-component ablations.

The noising interventions ablate dynamically selected multi-head circuits rather than single heads. The study tests one Llama family at the 1B scale, on synthetic tasks and a GSM8K proxy, not broad general text across model families and sizes.
The study reports differences across task classes and models, but not prompt-by-prompt variability or overcorrection beyond the original effect.
The paper proposes backup circuits as an explanation but does not separately identify and ablate backup heads or test copy-suppression heads, final LayerNorm rescaling, or anti-erasure neurons.
Tests resample ablation; does not compare mean ablation against zero ablation.
Does not directly evaluate attribution scores or compare them against a ground-truth account of a component's function.

reader_labels.reason: The Instruct model's 6.79% drop is notably larger than the Base model's 2.92%, qualifying the strength of compensation in this setting (r5, r11).
